translations.text: Of our holy father John Chrysostom.
A sermon for Holy Friday. Our labor of fasting has now come to an end.
And it ends with the cross. For where should a victorious struggle end,
if not at the monument of victory? For the cross is victorious.

He was struck [?] only once, yet he is always driving out demons. For where are the idol-temples, and the slaughter and waste of animals? Where are the idol altars [?] and the impious fire? All were put out by one thing: the holy blood fell.
And the cross stood firm: a mighty power, an invisible arrow, an immaterial medicine, a spring that relieves suffering, a glory subjected to scorn.

Even if I speak of other unheard-of things about Christ, even if I astonish the listener by proclaiming unheard-of miracles, I glory not so much in those things as in the cross. For example, I will say this:

Jesus came forth from a virgin. It is a great miracle to bypass marriage and break through the order of nature. But if there had been no cross, the first virgin of Paradise would not have been saved by her deeds.
But now, at the time of the cross, the first woman is saved, healing the ancient evil through new gifts of grace.
A dead man rose in Galilee, but he died again. But I, having risen because of the Cross, can no longer fall into death. Jesus, God, sailed the sea in a boat.

On that day the wood gave success, but I have received the wood, an eternal good. I took it in place of a spiritual ship, and with it I drive back the waves of the cunning ones. Five thousand were fed, not by any arrangement [?] of the cross. Where, then, are the leftovers of that food? How can I, who was not there, take the remnants of those who were there? For twelve baskets of fragments were left over.

For that gift of grace was limited in number. Christ was crucified, and we are continually fed. Even when we have eaten our fill, we ask again; having received, we love, and our need becomes greater. For grace is never depleted. Let this day be praised, the world's parent, because of which the other days were appointed for rejoicing. How? Listen. Today Adam was created, on the sixth day. Today he bore the divine image. Today a little world was formed within the world. Today the human helmsman, the good oars of the inhabited world,

a living creature ruling over all living creatures. Today he received commandments for the exercise of his free will. Today he fell out of Paradise. Today he was admitted again. O day of many forms! O day of many tears and of no tears! O day that brought sorrow in the morning but joy in the evening! Indeed, it did not do as much harm as it brought healing. I confess to you that I am sorrowful as I pursue the sufferings of old, hearing of Adam cast out of his Father's house: a man who was a citizen of Paradise, living without working the earth, fed without rain, needing no sweat or spade or toil or running about to sustain his life, delighting in evergreen trees, passing from flower to flower,
passing from fruit to fruit. Following
a thought, having need to follow it, but, because of the beauty of the things he saw, having no [?] toward which to stretch out his hands first. Many times I wept over such great blessings,
seeing him deprived of them.
For the suffering was shared and touched our race as well. But when I looked into the Gospels and came to this day—for that day was the sixth, and so is this one.
I have also done away with sorrow and been changed, and I am bright in my words. And I say to myself and to you: pain and sorrow and sighing have fled away.
The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.
For just as physicians' servants heal snakebites, taking healing remedies out of the snakes themselves, mixing them with wines, and curing the harm of the wounds,
so too the Saviour turned all evil causes to good, making human bitterness sweet.
turning it into healing, turning death’s sting back upon death itself, turning the injury caused by the tree into salvation, and taking away the day that had saddened the world.
and gave back a day that gladdened the world. Do not believe me, but your own eyes.
Look at this gathering, and stop [?] us with the day of the cross.
And let us all rejoice and fast from evil, and let us cleanse everything within and without. Such is the message of the feast; such is the form of its rejoicing.
I will tell a few of the wonders of the cross’s power. Look at the circle of the inhabited world:
how many villages and how many cities, how many places, how many nations, how many islands, how many rivers, how many coasts,

how many peoples, countries, and foreigners there are! They all fast because of the cross, having crucified their enemies through its power. For many, the night comes to an end, but the labor of fasting does not come to an end.
And now, why have we all gathered? To hear something about the Cross. We fill the church and push one another, sweating and toiling. Before judges we are often
deemed worthy of the front places.
But we stand gladly before Jesus, since Jesus stood for our sake, in order to stop the course of evil.
What, then, happened today? Let us not allow the wonders of this day simply to pass us by. For there was moonlight, and it was just before dawn.
And he was led, with his hands bound, into Pilate’s praetorium.
The hands that healed the blind and cured the lame, and the fingers, were bound fast with fetters.
He who fashioned eyelids, the healer of nature, was held back, so that he could not finish his skilful work.

Is this how you repay the Lord? He was bound—the one who binds the waters in the clouds and by his might releases those in chains. He who grants release to captives was bound, he who freed Lazarus from the bonds of death.
He was led into the prison: he who is attended by unknowable angels as his armour-bearers, he who has heaven as his throne.
And the Creator endured being dragged along by his creation,
The Creator by his creation, the Maker by what he had made. What, then, about these things?
What happened? And they, it says, did not go into the prison, so that they would not be defiled but might eat the great day.
O great lawlessness! The murderers commit injustice [?].
And they refuse to go into the prison, guarding themselves against being defiled,

they who were already defiled, slaughtering the sheep along with the sheep [?]. So he awaited judgment, the judge of the whole world. He awaited a witness, the witness of souls, the one who created them.
And he was judged, and men sat judging him.
But God stood, and as he stood he was silent. Standing before human doors was the master of the heavenly doors. Pilate questioned him, being, it seems, more humane than the Jews.

What shall I say? The deeds will indeed reveal the truth. What accusation do you bring against this man? Who can find God guilty? I am compelled to speak Pilate’s words. For Jesus is silent—not because the Word does not know how to speak, but lest by answering he undo the crown of the cross. Did he desire possessions, when he disregarded possessions? Other people’s houses, when he had nowhere to lay his head? Wealth, when he stripped even his own disciples down to their belts? Having no donkey, he took someone else’s donkey to bless your children. State the charge. Show whether you have put him to death justly. The Jews answered him:
"If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you." A great proof of his deeds! An answer without rule or reason.

Tell [me] the evil, and do not act deceitfully toward the listeners. Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves, and judge him according to your law." The wise judge laid the burden on the heads of the Jews: "You take the evil accomplice [?]." The Jews said to him, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death." How then did you kill Isaiah? How Zechariah? How each of the prophets? But "it is not for us to kill" was said not because they were unwilling, but because they were unable, for they no longer had such power, the Romans having taken it away. So the law is being destroyed, lying there now only as ink, idle in deeds. And the bound Jesus destroyed it. Pilate said, "I find no fault in him." Not you alone, O Pilate, but also neither the Jews, nor the blind, nor the dead, nor the sun, nor the moon, nor creation, nor all the righteous,

prophets and martyrs [find any]. The prophet says, "Who did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." All speak together with Pilate, giving him the name "righteous." Only the Jews oppose it, contending with shouting and wishing to overshadow the truth with clamor, and fulfilling Isaiah's words: "I waited for it to produce wine, but it produced thorns; and not righteousness, but a cry." An empty cry, the vineyard of the Jews,

bearing a cry as its fruit. While this was being done, Pilate could neither speak nor hear because of the tumult that had gathered, and he thought there would be an uprising. Then his wife, a good helper, sent to him, admonishing and restraining her husband, saying, "Have nothing to do with that righteous man." If you can, release him; if you cannot, keep yourself away from it. She all but spoke David's words:

"Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood." "Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him in a dream." She was another Joseph, seeing the truth in dreams and testifying against the cry of the Jews. For it was fitting that they be defeated by a woman. Rahab the harlot overcame them; the woman with the issue of blood overcame them; the Canaanite woman overcame them; and now again a woman prevails against them. The Jews answered him, "We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die." What law? By what words are you convinced? Perhaps by those read today: "He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb without malice is silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth. Because of the lawlessness of my people he was led to death." These I find to be necessary for those words [?].
But nowhere else. Jesus in [?]

…Righteousness being killed. Pilate went into the praetorium, giving free rein to the rage of the Jews. He tried to quench the unquenchable flame; he went in and came out, but instead he kindled the fire even more. For he came out leading Jesus crowned and clothed in purple: already the victor, already clothed in the likeness of a king. What was done was meant as mockery, but it was a figure of what kingship truly is. So they saw him whom they had seen many times, and yet saw him as they had never seen him. Always seeing him, they are set ablaze, burned by their own fire. It would have been better for them to have been burned up by fire. The Sodomite outcry roused them; they rose up and were carried away: "Take him, take him, crucify him!" "Shall I crucify your king?" "We have no king but Caesar," they said. A renunciation made without persecution; godlessness joined with Egyptian wickedness.
“Are these your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt?” Do you have no king but Caesar?
Who, then, led you through the wilderness? Who fed you? Whom does Moses acclaim when he says, “The Lord reigns forever and ever, and beyond”?
Since, then, you have rejected your own king, remain without a king,

dragging the everlasting yoke of slavery. This took place until the sixth hour. Let us also see the remaining part of the day, for all of it is holy. They took him, crowned. With what thorns? With Jewish
rewards. “I expected it to produce wine for me, but it produced thorns.” He was struck in the face.
He received blows, but was put to shame by nothing. Stand with Jesus and see that God with your eyes.
For what did he say? “Lord, who has believed our report? We saw him, and he had no form

or beauty. Rather, his appearance was dishonored, more disfigured than that of the sons of men.” Did the maker of all beauty have no beauty? For he mourned the wickedness of the Jews, being a man afflicted with wounds and knowing how to endure pain.
A man, not God.
For it was as a man, and not as God, that he was wounded.
Who, then, is this man of many pains and many troubles, rejected by everyone? Can it be that he suffers justly?
He bears our sins and accepts pain for us.
"I find no fault at all in this man." But he is not ashamed of the shameful benefits [?]. Having suffered so much, he remained beyond suffering. He was made manifest [?].

Spat upon, he received dishonor, and yet he himself remains honored and glorious. Of those who sin [?]… as one of them, Isaiah, said to them: "And we thought him to be in pain and in wounds and in affliction."
"But he was wounded for our sins, and he was in pain for our iniquities," so that he [?]… and we, who were wounded, were healed by his wound.
A dead man for the dead; a wounded physician for people suffering many ills; a remedy that works against the wound. But how long, O man, will you flatter [?] our freedom from suffering?
Say plainly what is being sought: "As a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb."

The good sheep, handed over to wicked cooks, is slaughtered. O Jews, do not shear the sheep; and if you do shear it, spare the sheep that brings good fruit. Others were also led with him, two evildoers. For our discourse comes to the tenth hour of the day [?]. Let no one condemn his own life. I meant to pass over the story, since I have told it to you many times, but I see the thief always pressing me. And no wonder: did he not force even the doors of paradise [?]? He skillfully took salvation away from us [?] by turning [?]… The lamb stood on the cross, and two wolves. One remained earthly in his ways, but the other was already being changed, saying: "Remember me when you come in your kingdom." O the power of Jesus! The thief is already a prophet, preaching from the cross: "Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom." What do you see that is royal, O thief?

The slaps, or the spitting? The nails, or the wood? The stumbling of the Jews, and the spear already drawn by the soldier? "But I see," he says, "his angels standing around; I see the sun fleeing, the veil being torn, the earth trembling, the dead already learning to flee. Jesus receiving all, who even to the one…" [the text breaks off]

hour, gave the same denarius. “Truly, truly, I say to you.” Receive this “truly” yourself, O robber: you who today are a robber, today are a son. “Today you will be with me in paradise. I, who drove you out, am bringing you in—I who closed the gates of paradise, who fenced it off with a flaming spear. For unless I bring you in, the gates will remain closed. Come, O robber, who have defeated the devil and been crowned over him, who have seen a man and worshiped God, who have thrown down your former weapon

and taken up a trustworthy one.” With things being so, and everything illuminated—the sun from the sky, the wood from the gardens, the gall from the Jews, the seamless robe from the woven fabrics, the purple for clothing from the sea, and the iron from the mines, the spear and the nails—and with the twin streams of blood and water poured out, the Savior was doing his work. “Father, forgive them their sin.” Whom was he to forgive? The Greeks or the Jews? Strangers or foreigners? Everyone without distinction. For he spoke once, and the deed is continually being done. [?] Was it only of the soldiers that he said, “Forgive”? He speaks throughout all ages, and he speaks continually, and whoever wishes receives. They all gathered in Pilate’s praetorium. What did they say? “We know that this deceiver said, while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise.’”
Do you know very well? Do you remember very well that he will rise? He secures the tomb. For you are securing it for me. Keep watch.

the dead man, so that he does not escape. “Do you have a guard?” he said. “Go and secure it as you know how. You killed him as you saw fit; make your arrangements as you know how. Keep watch. If you had not guarded him, you would have left grounds for an accusation against me. But now I hand him over to you yourselves. When he was alive, he was held by you; but when he was killed, he was hidden from you all.” Let us therefore remain watchful, not sleeping, so that we may see the deep sleep of the Jews and celebrate with the heavenly hosts in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and dominion, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
